artworks.title: Jupiter and Antiope (The Pardo Venus)
artworks.description: Titian's great Louvre canvas (also called the Pardo Venus) stages Zeus as a satyr unveiling the sleeping Theban Antiope — the encounter that begets Amphion and Zethus. It is the Renaissance's most famous image of this Antiope, not the Amazon queen.

artworks.title: Jupiter and Antiope (Nymph and Satyr)
artworks.description: Watteau's Louvre painting returns to the same Theban myth: a satyr-like Jupiter discovers the sleeping Antiope. The soft Rococo handling keeps the subject of Zeus' love for the mother of Amphion and Zethus.

artworks.title: Jupiter and Antiope
artworks.description: David's early canvas (Musées de Sens) shows Jupiter as satyr approaching the sleeping Antiope — a Neoclassical essay on the Theban mother whose twin sons will later avenge her against Dirce.

artworks.title: Farnese Bull
artworks.artist: Apollonius of Tralles and Tauriscus of Tralles (Roman copy)
artworks.year: c. late 2nd century BC (original type); Roman copy
artworks.description: The colossal Naples group shows Amphion and Zethus binding Dirce to the bull — the revenge that restores their mother, the Theban Antiope, after years of persecution. Antiope's story is the mythic hinge of antiquity's most famous Dirce monument.

popCulture.title: Antiope (mother of Amphion)
popCulture.description: The Theban Antiope endures as the oppressed mother of Amphion and Zethus — Zeus' beloved who fled, suffered under Dirce, and was avenged by her twin sons.

popCulture.title: Dirce
popCulture.description: Antiope's tormenter remains tied to the Farnese Bull — Dirce bound to the bull by Amphion and Zethus in one of antiquity's most famous revenge images.
